interviewQuestions.question: What is pipelining, and does it make an individual instruction execute faster?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by defining it as an overlap technique, not a speed-up-one-instruction technique. Pipelining splits instruction execution into stages built from separate hardware — fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back — so while one instruction is decoding, the next can already be fetching, and the one after that can already be fetching its own successor. Nothing shortens any single instruction's own journey through those stages; if anything, the pipeline registers latching data between stages add a small fixed overhead to each instruction's total latency, since a signal now has to be captured and released at every stage boundary rather than flowing straight through combinational logic.

What pipelining buys you instead is **throughput**: once the pipeline is full (after an initial fill delay of a few cycles), a new instruction can complete nearly every single cycle instead of every N cycles, where N was roughly the unpipelined instruction's total latency. I'd use the laundromat analogy to make this concrete — three machines running wash, dry, and fold on three different loads simultaneously finish far more loads of laundry per hour than one machine doing all three steps sequentially per load, but no single load of laundry gets washed and dried and folded any faster than before.

**Testing:** whether you distinguish latency from throughput — a very common trip-up when people first meet pipelining, and one that resurfaces constantly in later performance discussions.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Pipelining and instruction latency

interviewQuestions.question: For an N-stage pipeline, why is the achieved speedup always less than N?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Two reasons I'd cover. First, there's a fixed startup cost: filling the pipeline takes N-1 cycles before the first instruction fully completes, and this fill cost gets amortized over however many instructions run — for a short program it dominates and speedup stays well below N.

Second, and the bigger real-world factor, is hazards. Structural hazards (two instructions wanting the same hardware), data hazards (one instruction needs a result the previous one hasn't produced yet), and control hazards (branches whose target isn't known yet) all force stall cycles or bubbles, leaving stages idle instead of doing useful work. I'd close by noting that real CPUs spend a lot of design effort — forwarding, branch prediction, out-of-order execution — specifically clawing back this gap between ideal and real speedup.

**Testing:** whether you can name the concrete mechanisms (fill time, hazards) rather than just asserting "real life isn't ideal."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why ideal speedup isn't reached

interviewQuestions.question: If pipelining is such a good idea, why don't CPUs just keep adding more and more stages indefinitely?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd push back on the premise with the actual costs that grow as stage count grows, since 'more pipelining is always better' is exactly the intuition this question is checking for.

First, every extra stage boundary needs its own pipeline register, and each pipeline register adds fixed latch overhead — setup and hold time, clock skew margin — that eats into the per-stage time budget without doing any useful work itself; past a point, splitting work into ever-thinner stages returns diminishing clock-speed gains because the fixed overhead per stage becomes a larger fraction of an already-shrinking stage. Second, and usually the dominant real-world cost, deeper pipelines make every hazard more expensive: a branch misprediction now has to flush more in-flight instructions before the correct path is even fetched, since the branch resolves that many more stages downstream of fetch. The Pentium 4's roughly 20-31 stage pipeline is the textbook cautionary example — it hit very high clock speeds on paper, but real-world performance often lagged shallower-pipelined competitors because misprediction and stall penalties ate the clock-speed gains.

So stage count is a genuine design trade-off between clock speed and hazard cost, not a knob to maximize — which is exactly why the industry pulled back from the 'pipeline ever deeper' race after Pentium 4 and instead invested in wider issue, better branch prediction, and eventually more cores.

**Testing:** naming the two concrete costs (latch overhead, hazard cost growth) rather than a vague 'diminishing returns' hand-wave.
